clue.text: Walker — once got the push in this ?

definitions.text: once got the push in this

explanation.surface: A rambler recalls being shoved along as a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: one who perambulates is a walker. The second is the pram, the short form of the word, in which every solver was once pushed as a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler or stroller is a walker, and the full name of a baby's pram is the same word, so you were once pushed in one.

clue.text: Bird book

explanation.surface: A two-word note pairing a bird with reading matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Penguin is also the paperback publisher, so a Penguin is a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The flightless Antarctic seabird shares its name with the paperback imprint, so a paperback from that publisher is one.

clue.text: Go over it again — it gets one tired

explanation.surface: Doing the same thing twice is wearisome.
explanation.walkthrough: To tread again is to go over ground again; a remoulded tyre has a new tread, so it gets a vehicle re-tyred, punning on 'tired'.
explanation.definitionFit: To step over ground once more is to tread it again, and a remoulded tyre fitted to a wheel gives that wheel a fresh tyre.

clue.text: R.L.S. got her to do all the donkey work.

definitions.text: R.L.S. got her to do all the donkey work.

parts.words: R.L.S. got her to do all the donkey work.
parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson's Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes features the she-ass who carried his pack

explanation.surface: A writer made a woman do all the drudgery.
explanation.walkthrough: R.L.S. is Robert Louis Stevenson; 'donkey work' sounds like drudgery, but his donkey literally did the work, carrying his baggage in Travels with a Donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The she-ass Stevenson hired to carry his load across the Cevennes was named this, so she did his donkey work.

clue.text: Cruel sort of complaint

indicators.note: sort here is a verb, to sort out or rearrange, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A grumble about a nasty type of illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges CRUEL.
explanation.definitionFit: An open sore is a medical complaint, in the sense of an ailment.

clue.text: River in a small way is stirred up

indicators.note: in puts the river inside the letters for a small way

parts.note: RD, short for road, is a small way since it is abbreviated
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: A stream that is modestly agitated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts OUSE, a river in England, inside A RD, 'small way' meaning the abbreviation of road.
explanation.definitionFit: Feelings that are excited or provoked have been stirred up.

clue.text: Finished with double — to emulate the Hamelin Rats?

parts.note: over means finished, as in the game is over
to double is to run, as in at the double

explanation.surface: A double act finishes by copying the rats of Hamelin.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Pied Piper story the town of Hamelin was overrun by rats; 'double' is a verb, to move at the double.
explanation.definitionFit: The rats swarmed through Hamelin, so to swarm over a place as they did is the verb meant.

clue.text: A player may find it cushy and take pot-luck

definitions.text: A player may find it cushy and take pot-luck

parts.words: A player may find it cushy and take pot-luck
parts.note: cushy suggests easy but means hitting the table's cushion, and pot-luck means a chance shot sinking into a pocket

explanation.surface: A sportsman finds things easy and trusts to chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cushy' and 'pot-luck' read as idioms for easy and chancy, but a ball on a baize table strikes the cushions and may be potted by luck.
explanation.definitionFit: On a baize table the player's object strikes cushions and is potted, sometimes by a lucky shot.

clue.text: Editing managed to make things hot

indicators.note: managed here means handled or worked over, so the letters of the fodder are rearranged

explanation.surface: A piece of editing stirred up controversy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'managed' tells you to rework the letters of EDITING; 'to make things' links the anagram to the definition 'hot', in the sense of set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set alight and burning is hot, so a kindled fire is a synonym in that sense.

clue.text: Suffer defeat in football : match—-camera shot

indicators.note: in places the losing word inside the match word

parts.note: a cup tie is a football match, giving CUP
to suffer defeat is to lose

explanation.surface: A team loses its match and the photographer gets the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts LOSE inside CUP, a knockout football match.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph or film frame taken from very near the subject is a type of camera shot.

clue.text: Worker getting water has five cents for bread

parts.note: one who pumps up water is a pumper
a nickel is the US five-cent coin

explanation.surface: A labourer fetching water carries small change for a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' joins the two pieces; the definition is the dark German rye loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: The dense dark rye loaf from Westphalia is a kind of bread.

clue.text: Honours gained are not Hardy's

explanation.surface: A note on awards that went to one comedian and not his partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurel and Hardy were a comedy double act; what is not Hardy's is Laurel's. The other sense is honours, from the laurel wreath awarded to victors.
explanation.definitionFit: Wreaths of bay given to victors stand for honours won, and things not belonging to Hardy belong to his partner Stan Laurel.

clue.text: Platform for a Latin beak

explanation.surface: A speaker's stage named after a bird's bill in Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: In Latin the word means a beak; the Roman speaking platform was decorated with the beaks of captured ships, hence its English sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised stand for a speaker or conductor is a platform, and the Latin noun for a bird's bill or ship's prow is the same word.

clue.text: Sheltered by a West End arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement of letters is a rearranging of them, the anagram signal

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Somewhere in the West End of London, people take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's theatre district, but here it splits into W and END, which with A are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitted with an awning, a canvas canopy, a shopfront is sheltered from sun and rain.

clue.text: It added to the dignity of Landseer's painting

definitions.text: It added to the dignity of Landseer's painting

parts.words: It added to the dignity of Landseer's painting
parts.note: Landseer's famous painting of two dogs is titled with 'Dignity and' followed by a second noun meaning cheek

explanation.surface: Something made a Victorian painter's work look grander.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edwin Landseer painted two dogs as 'Dignity and Impudence'; the word added to 'Dignity' in the title is the answer, though the surface suggests something lending a painting grandeur.
explanation.definitionFit: The painting's title joins this word to Dignity, so it is literally what was added to the dignity.

clue.text: Fleet (Street) mob ?

parts.note: a gang seizing men for the navy's fleet, and with Street added a mob of Fleet Street journalists, the press

explanation.surface: A crowd of newspaper hacks on London's Fleet Street.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street was London's newspaper district, so its mob is the press; without the bracketed word, the fleet's mob forcibly recruited sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: A band that forcibly enlisted men into the fleet was so named, and a mob of journalists is literally the press in a gang.

clue.text: Type of sword dance, same but different

indicators.note: different says the combined letters come out in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Highland-style sword dance that is identical yet not identical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sword dance' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'sword'; 'different' rearranges DANCE and SAME.
explanation.definitionFit: Blades made in Damascus, with their wavy watered steel, give their name to a type of sword.

clue.text: Butter up two points the green light for battle!

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a ram is an animal that butts, a butter
E and N are two compass points, east and north
the green light means go

explanation.surface: Flattery and two tips act as a signal to start the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter up' reads as flatter, but Butter is one who butts, a RAM, turned to MAR by 'up'. Marengo was Napoleon's 1800 victory.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon defeated the Austrians at Marengo in 1800, so it names a battle.

clue.text: Scuttle-fish ?

explanation.surface: A sea creature that runs off in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: A seacock is a valve in a ship's hull that can be opened to scuttle, or sink, the vessel; the sea cock is also a name for the gurnard.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening a hull valve sinks a ship deliberately, and the gurnard, a spiny sea creature, is also called by this name.

clue.text: Meaty essayist

explanation.surface: A writer described as having substance.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Bacon wrote famous Essays; the other sense is the cured pig meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cured pork is meaty fare, and Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan philosopher, was a celebrated essayist.

clue.text: First class vessel sailor brought up from Jakarta once

indicators.note: in a down clue brought up means the run of pieces reads from bottom to top

parts.note: A1, written AI, means first class
a vat is a vessel for liquid
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A fine ship with its seaman sails up from Indonesia's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' turns AI VAT AB into BATAVIA; A1 is written with the letter I standing for the figure 1.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch colonial name for the city now called Jakarta was Batavia, so it was Jakarta's former name.

clue.text: Some recent research in chocolates

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A little new research into chocolates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes the run from receNT RESearch... reCENT RESearch gives the answer, what lies in the middle of chocolates.
explanation.definitionFit: A filled chocolate has a soft or creamy core, and those fillings are what lie in chocolates.

clue.text: Companies concerned in keeping up their overheads.?

definitions.text: Companies concerned in keeping up their overheads

parts.words: Companies concerned in keeping up their overheads
parts.note: overheads looks like business costs but means things flying overhead, which airline firms keep aloft

explanation.surface: Firms worried about controlling their running costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overheads' suggests an accountant's costs; read literally, it is aircraft in the sky, which airline companies keep up. The grid as held prints a near-twin.
explanation.definitionFit: Airline companies operate flights, so their business is keeping aircraft up overhead.

clue.text: Material — how students pro, tested?

explanation.surface: A fabric connected with student demonstrations.
explanation.walkthrough: Students staged sit-ins, so they 'sat in'; written as one word it is the glossy fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossy silk cloth is a material, and protesters occupying a building sat in it.

clue.text: "Can't" is a terribly devilish word

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly done, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe giving no letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone declares that saying 'can't' is a wicked thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges CANT IS A; 'word' at the end is filler pointing to the definition 'devilish'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of the Devil, Satan, is devilish.

clue.text: What the moving finger wrote cancelled at Rugby?

definitions.text: What the moving finger wrote cancelled at Rugby?

parts.words: What the moving finger wrote cancelled at Rugby?
parts.note: a written row of words struck through is a line cancelled, and the rugby restart with throw-in between two rows of forwards has the same name

explanation.surface: A line from the Rubaiyat about the moving finger, applied to Rugby School.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam says no tears can wash out a word the moving finger writes; a line written and struck out is 'line out', and at rugby a lineout restarts play.
explanation.definitionFit: A written line deleted is put out, and at rugby the set-piece throw from touch carries the same name.

clue.text: Unfavourable publicity lines

parts.note: an ad is publicity for a product
verse is lines of poetry

explanation.surface: Bad press in a few lines of print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfavourable publicity' looks like one phrase, but 'publicity' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Conditions that work against you are hostile or unfavourable.

clue.text: Through which one read of the slaying of the Jabberwock

definitions.text: Through which one read of the slaying of the Jabberwock

parts.words: Through which one read of the slaying of the Jabberwock
parts.note: the Jabberwocky poem appears in Lewis Carroll's sequel whose title begins with the word Through, and it is printed in mirror writing

explanation.surface: Where a reader came across the poem about killing a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jabberwocky' is in Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass, and Alice must hold it up to a mirror to read it, so one literally reads it through the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirror is what Alice reads the mirror-printed poem through, and the book holding it is named for that mirror.
